source.title: Andalusian carob handbook · UCOPress, 2026
source.authors: Rafael M. Navarro Cerrillo and Guillermo Palacios Rodríguez (editors)
source.research: LEARN-008: Carob Restoration — Nursery Buying Guide and Mixed Planting Models; LEARN-007: Soil Preparation and Growth with Limited Water.

features.label: Root collar
features.text: The transition between stem and roots belongs at the intended final soil surface. A deeper prepared area does not mean burying the collar deeper. Allow for settlement and avoid collecting water directly against the stem.
features.basis: Installation synthesis in LEARN-007; the handbook’s deep-preparation guidance concerns the soil around the plant.

features.label: Root ball
features.text: Remove the container and preserve the coherent root ball. Carob’s lateral roots are fragile. Inspect representative plants for healthy branching roots and reject coiled, damaged or decaying root systems.

features.label: Final soil surface
features.text: Use the final, settled local soil level as the reference for positioning the plant. A rainfall-capture basin is a separate design decision: check infiltration, overflow and drainage before changing the surface.
features.basis: Planting-position synthesis in LEARN-007 combined with the MR2 microcatchment discussion.

features.label: Stable support
features.text: Support the root ball so it will retain its intended level after watering and settlement. Deep preparation needs stable soil beneath the ball; a loose organic bed can settle. The drawing is not a prescription for a concrete pad or an impermeable layer.
features.basis: Soil preparation and settlement synthesis in LEARN-007; not a measured finca section.

features.label: Preparation depth
features.text: Preparation can extend below and beside the root ball to provide connected, usable soil. Choose it from the actual soil profile, restrictions and drainage. MR2 describes 60 × 60 × 60 cm holes; that is a model recommendation, not a universal optimum or a root-collar burial depth.
features.basis: General preparation guidance and the oasification model.

features.label: Root-ball dimensions
features.text: Measure the actual root-ball width and height. Nominal litres do not determine its shape, and the handbook provides no validated litres-to-hole-size conversion. A 1 L container does not automatically imply a 40 cm or 60 cm hole.
features.basis: Comparison of container formats and reported preparation examples; no formula is established.

preparations.title: 40 × 40 × 40 cm · Las Labores, Albox
preparations.text: Manual holes for nursery plants about 1 m tall, in former almond/olive land. Container dimensions are not given. The site received summer drip water and later grafting; it is a partial match to an ungrafted mixed restoration project.

preparations.title: 60 × 60 × 60 cm · MR2 oasification
preparations.text: A preparation recommendation for low-density restoration using rainfall capture, microcatchments and stone mulch. Support watering remains part of the model. It is not a controlled trial comparing hole sizes.

buying_checks.title: Seed-grown and ungrafted
buying_checks.text: Ask for planta de semilla sin injertar. A seed-grown rootstock with a graft is still a grafted plant. Micropropagation is laboratory tissue multiplication, generally used for clones; it is not needed for this seed-based approach.

buying_checks.title: Known provenance and diversity
buying_checks.text: Request seed collection origin and batch traceability; ask whether material came from multiple parent trees. The nursery’s address alone does not establish the seed’s origin.

buying_checks.title: Healthy, branching roots
buying_checks.text: Inspect representative plants out of their pots. Look for fine lateral roots and reject spiralling, hooked, severely damaged or decaying roots. A larger pot cannot correct malformed roots.

buying_checks.title: An intact, balanced plant
buying_checks.text: The plug should hold together without being pot-bound. Consider collar diameter and shoot balance, not height alone. Check healthy foliage and the absence of drying, mould and disease.

buying_checks.title: Hardened and ready for the site
buying_checks.text: Ask about outdoor acclimation, irrigation conditioning, nutrition and time in the current container. Coordinate delivery with a favourable planting window.

containers.label: Conventional forestry format
containers.text: Reported for short-cycle seed-grown restoration stock and in the MR1/MR2 tables. Quality and establishment conditions still matter.

containers.label: Candidate for the pilot
containers.text: Listed in the short-cycle nursery programme; also used by the local Níjar supply specification reviewed in LEARN-008. A practical candidate to discuss with the nursery, not a proven growth or water-use optimum.

containers.label: Larger-stock alternative
containers.text: Discussed for higher functional quality and rootstock production. MR2’s narrative favours stock above 1 L, while its table lists smaller stock. Inspect roots, cost and care needs before choosing.

substrate.title: Choose properties, not one universal recipe
substrate.text: Ask for an aerated, structurally stable nursery medium that retains available water and supports healthy fine roots and a coherent plug. The book lists peat/coir/bark bases with mineral components such as perlite or vermiculite, but its recipes differ by context. Ask for the actual mix and nutrient history. Nursery medium is not a field-pit backfill recipe.

care.title: Plant in a favourable moisture window
care.text: Favour autumn or early winter with suitable soil moisture, while checking the actual frost risk. The book describes 3–5 years of establishment care; planting is the beginning of that period.

care.title: Protect and inspect
care.text: Assess browsing, sun exposure, protector ventilation and competing vegetation around young plants. Retain valuable native vegetation elsewhere; restoration does not imply clearing the whole parcel.

care.title: Minimum and optimum water remain unresolved
care.text: There is no verified universal litres-per-week schedule, minimum volume or stopping date for our seedlings. Use site observations, a measured external-water budget and a defined rescue rule. Established drought-tolerant trees do not establish a zero-water protocol for new stock.

care.title: Reported carob survival · Almería: 40–60%
care.text: On p. 124, the handbook reports 40–60% survival in Almería, citing Planelles et al. (2001) in its discussion of afforestation experience. It also reports 18–30% in Guadiamar and 0–65% in Córdoba, showing substantial variation between settings. The passage does not specify the monitoring period or enough trial conditions to transfer these figures to this parcel. These are historical reported results, not a predicted survival rate, an annual survival probability or a result for all companion species. Keep them separate from the later Las Labores, Albox case, which describes low mortality without a numeric estimate. No survival default or simulation effect is applied.

care.title: 400 L/tree over May–September · Albox example
care.text: Las Labores reports this total summer-period drip volume per tree. Event volumes, frequency and the end of irrigation are not fully specified. It is a finca observation, not a recommendation or a minimum for this project.

treatments.title: Nursery nutrition
treatments.text: Buy appropriately nourished stock. The nursery chapter reports controlled-release alternatives of 16-8-9 at 3.5 g product/L substrate, or 9-13-18 at 5 g product/L substrate. These are separate nursery examples, not combined doses, elemental-nutrient amounts or field irrigation concentrations. Product release time, water quality and medium matter; these examples do not form a complete feeding programme.

treatments.title: Optional field fertilizer
treatments.text: MR1 and MR2 generally omit routine field fertilizer. If testing nutrition for growth, first identify a limitation, obtain a justified local product/dose recommendation, and compare with untreated plants under the same water rules. No validated field dose is established for this parcel; do not multiply a nursery rate through a large field pit.

treatments.title: Mycorrhization · roots and beneficial fungi
treatments.text: Micorrización establishes a root–fungus association that can improve nutrient access and drought response. It is different from fertilizer and nitrogen-fixing nodules. Carob research includes arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF); greenhouse benefits do not guarantee field results. Ask the nursery which fungi were used and whether colonization was checked. The book’s mixed AMF/truffle discussion is not a generic inoculum recipe.

examples.title: Las Labores · Albox
examples.vegetation: Declining almond/olive land converted toward carob on shallow, rocky calcareous soil.
examples.water: 400 L/tree over the reported May–September period; an ongoing seasonal drip example, not a zero-water trial.
examples.management: Manual 40 cm cube holes, protectors, occasional tillage, pruning and later grafting.
examples.lesson: Useful management comparison, but only a partial match to mixed, ungrafted restoration. Low mortality is described without a numeric survival estimate or a control.

photo.alt: Original photograph of the carob planting at Las Labores, Albox, with trees on open cultivated ground.

examples.title: La Alcantarilla · Mojácar
examples.vegetation: Seminatural carob around houses and a stream, with lentisk and wild olive establishing beneath and around it.
examples.water: Original establishment water is not documented; favourable runoff locations do not prove zero irrigation.
examples.management: Limited later care beyond fruit collection; spread along roads, channels and streams.
examples.lesson: Strong reference for carob with shrubs and redistributed rainfall. No original container, hole-size or seedling survival protocol is given.

photo.alt: Original photograph of carob-associated vegetation around buildings at La Alcantarilla, Mojácar.

examples.title: La Tórtola · Níjar
examples.vegetation: Naturalized carob, lentisk and wild olive following former agricultural and grazing uses.
examples.water: No quantified establishment-water history; no cultural treatments reported for the described naturalized population.
examples.management: Irregular trees of different sizes, with very variable and generally negligible fruit production.
examples.lesson: A local vegetation reference, not a controlled planting trial or a growth forecast for newly purchased seedlings.

photo.alt: Original photograph of naturalized carob and shrub vegetation at La Tórtola, Níjar.

oak.title: Carob, oak and shrubs together
oak.text: Mixed oak–carob dehesas and MR1 support this landscape idea. Their wetter examples do not prove oak suitability across a dry Almería parcel. Assess oak taxon, provenance, soil depth, exposure and water separately; consider only suitable pockets and retain valuable shrub/open habitat.

photo.alt: Original photograph of a mixed holm-oak dehesa with carob trees.

limitations: Container volumes and seedling heights differ between the nursery narrative and restoration tables. No universally optimal stock class is established.
Substrate formulations vary by context; some long-cycle recommendations conflict. No universal nursery or field-backfill mix is adopted.
The general MR1 table says no irrigation; MR2 allows support water; Albox reports seasonal drip. These situations cannot be combined into one watering schedule.
Albox’s grafting dates, post-graft production account and fruit-sample year are inconsistent. Do not infer a time-to-fruiting forecast.
Low whole-parcel densities and closer spacing within planting groups use different area bases. No plant count or spacing is calculated here.
The book reports mostly 2023–2024 finca observations. Its 2026 publication date does not mean these sites were revisited in 2026.
The diagram is a conceptual teaching section, not measured roots, a mature rooting-depth estimate or a site execution specification.
